scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Dance of the Conquest: A 400-Year-Old Reenactment
This is Baile de la Conquista. 16th century.
on_screen: Title card: Baile de la Conquista · Guatemala · 16th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance was introduced by Dominican friars in the 16th century as a means of religious conversion.
It is an adaptation of the Spanish 'Baile de los Moros', utilizing the same structural framework of conflict and resolution through religious conversion.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed to honor a town's patron saint and serves as a psychological and cultural reenactment of the conquest, ultimately symbolizing the victory of Christianity.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: File:Danza de la conquista en Actopan Veracruz.webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9a/Danza_de_la_conquista_en_Actopan_Veracruz.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance involves 19 male performers arranged in three rows.
The center row includes the King and royal family; the first row contains the K'iche' chieftains; the second row contains the Spanish officers.
Movement is cyclical and repetitive, lasting approximately four hours.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is described as monotonous and cyclical.
The primary instruments are the chirimía and the drum.
Listen for the Chirimía, Drum, Marimba.
The music is characterized by the repetitive, cyclical sound of the chirimía and drum, with specific melodies assigned to different characters and circumstances.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear elaborate velvet capes, trousers, and masks.
Spanish characters wear pink masks with blonde hair and serious expressions.
Indigenous characters wear brown masks with smiling expressions.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Pedro de Alvarado (Spanish conquistador) and Tecun Uman (K'iche' leader).
Variations exist throughout Latin America, including the 'Danza de la Conquista' in southeastern Mexico, where women sometimes participate.
Directly descended from the Spanish 'Baile de los Moros'.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The dance is a significant cultural and religious performance often tied to patron saint festivals; outsiders should observe with respect and follow local protocols regarding photography and participation.
